spoken: On the evening of the 22nd of October 1956, students in Budapest drew up a list of sixteen demands.
The first broke a taboo that even that year's boldest debates had kept. It demanded that all Soviet troops leave Hungary.
Three and a half years earlier, Hungary had been a land of internment camps, show trials and fear.
This is the road between, from Stalin's death in March 1953 to the eve of the revolution.
On the 5th of March 1953, Joseph Stalin died, and his heirs in Moscow wanted calm in the countries they controlled.
Hungary worried them. Since 1949, wage earners' real wages had fallen by a fifth, and the economy was near collapse.
In June, they summoned Hungary's leaders to Moscow and condemned Mah-chahsh Rah-koshee's policies to his face.
Moscow's choice for prime minister was Im-reh Nodge, the Communist who had carried out the land reform of 1945.
On the 4th of July 1953, Nodge announced a new course in Parliament. For once, the country heard it from the government.
The internment camps were closed, the deportations ended, and an amnesty set many prisoners free.
Money moved from heavy industry to food and housing, and peasants could leave the collective farms.
The party's own reports told of villages lighting bonfires and celebrating Nodge until dawn.
By 1954, people consumed a fifth more than in 1950, and the web of terror, as one historian wrote, began to come apart.
But Rah-koshee stayed First Secretary of the party, and the party still ran the press, the radio and the officials.
Hungary now had two centres of power, and from the first day, Rah-koshee worked to win his back.
Many victims of the show trials were freed, among them Yah-nosh Kah-dahr, but Lahsloh Royk's case stayed taboo.
In Moscow in January 1955, Nodge said he could not work with Rah-koshee, and the Soviet leaders branded him anti-party.
In April, the party stripped him of his posts, and Rah-koshee's man, Andrash Heggedoosh, became prime minister.
Nodge refused to recant, and in December 1955 he was expelled from the party.
The old course returned, with more for heavy industry, heavier deliveries, and new pressure to join the collective farms.
But the old fear did not. Prisoners kept coming home, and writers began to protest against the party's control.
Next door, 1955 went the other way. On the 14th of May, Hungary signed the Warsaw Pact, an alliance under a Soviet commander.
The next day, the Austrian State Treaty ended the occupation of Austria, which soon declared itself neutral.
Since 1947, Soviet troops had stayed in Hungary to guard their lines to Austria. Many expected them to go, but they stayed.
On the 25th of February 1956, Nikita Khrushchev denounced Stalin's crimes in a secret speech to the Soviet party congress.
He spoke of the mass arrests and executions of party members, and of the cult of one leader.
For Rah-koshee, who had copied Stalin's cult in Hungary, it was a trap. He had to expose crimes he was responsible for.
In March, he had to admit that Lahsloh Royk, hanged in 1949, had been condemned on fabricated charges.
Debate moved to the Pet-urfee Circle, a club of the party's youth league, named after the poet of 1848.
On the 18th of June, Royk's widow, Yoolia, rose before the Circle and asked for her husband's name to be cleared.
On the 27th of June, a debate on the press filled the army officers' club, and loudspeakers carried it to the crowd outside.
About 6,000 people came, by the chairman's count. They stayed until half past one in the morning, and called for Nodge's return.
The Soviet ambassador, Yuri Andropov, reported that it had turned into a demonstration against the party leadership.
The next day, in Poz-nahn in Poland, workers marched for better pay and conditions. Security forces fired, and dozens were killed.
On the 30th of June, Hungary's party leadership condemned the Pet-urfee Circle, and its debates stopped.
Moscow feared trouble in Hungary too. In July, it sent one of its leaders, Anastas Mikoyan, to Budapest.
On the 18th of July, Rah-koshee resigned, citing his health and his mistakes, and soon left for the Soviet Union.
His successor as First Secretary was Airnuh Gairuh, who had run the economy at Rah-koshee's side for years.
New men such as Yah-nosh Kah-dahr joined the leadership, but the American Legation reported that the old gang was still there.
Gairuh named the Pet-urfee Circle among the enemy's tools, yet his leadership no longer had the strength to crack down.
Life stayed hard. By a trade union survey, more than half of all families with three children lived below the subsistence minimum.
On the 6th of October 1956, the anniversary of the martyrs of Arad, four coffins stood in the Keh-reh-peh-shee cemetery in Budapest.
Lahsloh Royk was reburied with three other victims of the same trials, Teebor Surnyee, Ondrahsh Sollo-ee and Dyurdy Pahlfee.
A huge crowd came. Estimates run from 100,000 to 350,000 people.
Bay-lah Sahss, once tried with Royk, said they had come not only to honour the dead, but to bury an era.
Im-reh Nodge offered his sympathy to Yoolia Royk, and that afternoon, students marched through the city centre against Stalinism.
On the 14th of October, the party took Nodge back, but gave him no place in government.
On the 16th of October, students in Seggaid left the party's youth league and founded their own union, Meffess, with leaders they chose themselves.
On the 19th of October, Soviet leaders flew unannounced to Warsaw, where Poland's party was changing course.
On the 21st of October, Go-moolka was elected party leader there, and Moscow gave way.
For Hungarians, the UN committee later wrote, this was the catalyst they had been half consciously waiting for.
On Monday, the 22nd of October, more than 2,000 people filled the great hall of the Technical University in Budapest.
They voted to join Meffess, and through the evening their list of demands grew from ten points to fourteen, then sixteen.
Point one demanded the immediate withdrawal of all Soviet troops, under the peace treaty.
They wanted a new government under Im-reh Nodge, and free elections with several parties.
Rah-koshee was to be tried, the press and radio set free, the Stalin statue taken down, and the Koh-shoot coat of arms restored.
The Pet-urfee Circle had never touched two taboos, the Soviet troops and the one-party state. The students broke both.
That evening, the radio refused to broadcast the demands in full, and the students would not let them be cut.
So the text was dictated into a microphone, written down in the hall, and copied by hand and typewriter across the city.
The Writers' Union meant to lay a wreath at the statue of General Bem, a Pole who fought for Hungary in 1848 and 1849.
The students called a silent march there for the next afternoon, in sympathy with Poland.
Three and a half years had led here, through a new course and its fall, a secret speech, a funeral, and sixteen points.
The country would not go on living the old way, a historian writes, and the regime no longer had the strength to defend it.
The next afternoon, the students marched. What followed was a revolution and a freedom fight.
